volatile

/VAH-luh-til/ — rhymes with bottle · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Volatile describes something likely to change suddenly and unpredictably, often violently.

The volatile stock doubled in May and crashed in June.

Example

After a political scandal breaks, the senator's approval rating swings violently — soaring to 60% one week, plummeting to 30% the next — making any prediction about the election outcome impossible.

Volatile is more precise than 'unstable' because it emphasizes sudden, dramatic, often violent shifts rather than mere uncertainty or lack of firmness. The rapid, unpredictable swings are the essence of volatility.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

unstable: Unstable means not steady - likely to shift, tip over, or collapse, like a wobbly chair or a shaky government. It warns that something may give way. Volatile warns of something different: sudden, dramatic swings, where a mood or a price can flip violently without notice.

turbulent: Turbulent describes violent, churning motion or unrest happening right now - turbulent air rattles a plane, a turbulent year is full of conflict. Volatile is about what could happen next: a volatile situation may look calm this minute and swing wildly the next.

explosive: Explosive points to one sudden, violent burst - an explosive temper goes off like a charge, all at once. Volatile describes the ongoing condition behind such bursts: liable to keep swinging suddenly and unpredictably, up and down, again and again over time.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

stable: steady, firmly settled, unlikely to change

predictable: behaving exactly as one would expect

Where it sits · how suddenly it can swing — steady → uneven → erratic → volatile

steady vs. volatile: Steady sits at the calm end of the scale — the very opposite of volatile — describing something that holds its course without any sudden change.

uneven vs. volatile: Uneven is only mildly unstable compared with volatile: an uneven performance wobbles a little, while a volatile one can swing wildly without warning.

erratic vs. volatile: Erratic is strong, but volatile is stronger; erratic behavior follows no pattern, while volatile behavior threatens to erupt into sudden, dramatic change at any moment.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — vol

Root — vol: to fly (Latin)

Suffix — -atile

Suffix — -atile: able to; tending to (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: In Latin, volatilis meant 'able to fly' — the root vol- 'to fly' plus the adjective suffix -atile. Something volatile can 'fly off' at any moment: it changes suddenly and unpredictably, the way a volatile liquid evaporates into the air.

Use the root in a new word: volley

Use the root in a new word: volley: The archers released a volley of arrows that flew through the air all at once — the same Latin root vol-, 'to fly,' that hides inside volatile.

Word Choice

formal / financial

Volatile is a strong word suggesting sudden, often violent shifts in condition or value. It is common in finance and chemistry, but also describes turbulent emotions or situations. Reserve it for truly erratic, dramatic change. For mild fluctuation or inconsistency, 'uneven' or 'unsteady' is more measured.
